_note: Element cards (issue #24). Every 'measured' item must link to its evidence; every prediction must link to the record written before its test. 'where' is description, not measurement. Built into the table by table/build_cards.py.

Vb.sentence: A regular wobble in the pitch of a held note, about five to seven times a second.
where: Classical and operatic singing, on long notes
Violin, viola and cello: the finger rocks on the string
Guitar, with a bending finger or a tremolo arm
Synthesizer leads, with a slow oscillator on the pitch
place: Column: Periodicity. It asks what repeats, and how often, but of the pitch track rather than of the raw sound. That makes it a second-order element, built on Pitch (F0).
Row: Event (Z 10.7 to 13). One wobble takes 0.15 to 0.18 s: too slow to be heard as a pitch of its own, too fast to tap along to.

Expected, not yet measured: played about five times faster, a vibrato crosses 20 wobbles a second and stops sounding like a wobble. It becomes a roughness of the tone, in the Tone row. Played much slower, it becomes a slow drift of pitch.

listen.label: A held melody with a 5.5 Hz vibrato of ±40 cents. Switch it off to hear the same notes straight.

found.summary: We tracked the pitch of every held note, removed the note itself, and looked for a regular swing in what was left. Each one-second window was judged on its own, by the same gate for every recording.

chart.title: Vibrato rate found, median and 10–90% range

numbers: Every solo recording lands in the Event row: Z 12.29 to 12.50.
The piano without vibrato gave no false alarms; a 5.5 Hz vibrato written into it was found at 5.51 Hz.
Voices swing wider than the violin: ±30 to 40 cents against ±13.
limits: Inside a mix it is not solved yet: a violin with piano and a cello with orchestra gave no vibrato windows.
The Suno voices carry vibrato on only 11 to 16% of their held-note time, mostly late in long notes.

predictions.text: Vibrato lives in the Event row (Z 10.7 to 13).
predictions.fail: A natural vibrato read outside the row, slower than 4 or faster than 20 wobbles a second (the borders of the row).
predictions.evidence: Predicted by the second edition of the table before the measurement; measured at Z 12.29 to 12.50.

predictions.text: Generated singing starts its vibrato late in a long note, which makes it a fingerprint of generation.
predictions.fail: A human reference singer shows the same late start.
predictions.evidence: Seen in two Suno voices; no human reference recording yet.

predictions.text: Vibrato can be read inside a full mix, not only on a solo stem.
predictions.fail: No method finds it in a mix where it is known to be present.
predictions.evidence: Not found yet in the two mixes tried.

Vb.pharmakon: Not in PHARMAKON yet. Measured in this project.

F0.sentence: The note you hear: how many times a second the waveform repeats. A4 repeats 440 times a second.
where: Every melody and bass line
A sung or spoken voice
Any instrument that plays a note rather than a noise
place: Column: Periodicity. It asks what repeats, and how often, of the raw waveform.
Row: Tone (Z 6 to 10.7). A note's period is 2 to 50 ms. Faster than about 20 repeats a second, repeats are heard as pitch.
Measured: play a drum loop 32 times faster and its rhythm turns into a note of this row, five rows below the pulse. Rhythm and pitch are the same question at different speeds.

listen.label: The collider's melody alone: eight held notes, no vibrato.

found.summary: We followed the waveform period frame by frame on the bass and lead-vocal stems of three tracks, keeping only the frames where the period was clear.

chart.title: Pitch found, as Z (10th to 90th percentile)

numbers: Every bass and vocal median lands in the Tone row.
The highest vocal notes cross into the Wave row (Z below 6), as the Z rule says they should.
Time compression: drums played 32 times faster gave a note whose period, times 32, was 2.00, 2.00 and 1.00 pulses (within 0.3%).
limits: The Metro vocal stem is almost silent (voiced in under 0.1% of frames), so it is left out.

predictions.text: Pitch lives in the Tone row.
predictions.fail: A bass or vocal median outside Z 6 to 10.7.
predictions.evidence: Predicted by the second edition before measuring; all five medians are in the row.

predictions.text: A rhythm played fast enough becomes a pitch of the same column.
predictions.fail: The compressed drums give a note that is not a whole number of pulses.

F0.pharmakon: Used inside the tempo and chroma analysis; there is no pitch tracker for melody or bass in PHARMAKON yet.

Pu.sentence: The beat you tap your foot to. Its rate is the tempo, and 120 BPM is exactly Z 14.
where: The kick of a four-on-the-floor dance track
The kick and snare of rock and hip-hop
The bass and chords of music without drums
place: Column: Periodicity. It asks what repeats, and how often, of the onsets.
Row: Beat (Z 13 to 16), 0.25 to 2 s: the range in which a pulse can be felt and tapped.
It is the reference of the metric axis. Bars, subdivisions and chord changes are counted from it.

listen.label: A kick on every beat with a hat between, at 110 BPM. Switch the pulse off to hear the rest of the sound without it.

found.summary: We took the onset curve of the drums, looked for its best period, and accepted it only after four tests: significance against the noise level, enough repetitions, stability in both halves, and a correlation that falls and returns.

chart.title: Tempo found on the real drum stems

numbers: The pulse is confirmed on every real drum stem, at 42 to 116 standard deviations above the noise level.
On noise and on shuffled drums, no pulse is confirmed (0% false periods held out).
On a strict benchmark the rule is exact on 76.5 to 80% of beats; the rest are bars or half bars.
limits: The level is not always right: on a 174 BPM breakbeat and on a fast waltz the rule returns the bar, not the beat. A better rule is a candidate, not yet in the core code.

predictions.text: A pulse lives in the Beat row.
predictions.fail: A confirmed pulse slower than 30 or faster than 240 BPM.
predictions.evidence: Every confirmed pulse is in the row.

predictions.text: A rule can be found that returns the beat itself, not its bar or its half.
predictions.fail: No rule passes real recordings with verified beat labels.
predictions.evidence: A candidate gets 94 to 95% on two held-out sets; real labels are the next step (issue #15).

Pu.pharmakon: Tempo in the Track Map: multi-band onsets with octave and meter checks.

Sc.sentence: The whole mix ducks on every kick and swells back, so the track seems to breathe.
where: House, EDM and French touch, on pads and bass
Pop productions that keep the kick clear of the bass
place: Column: Periodicity, asked of the level track rather than of the sound. That makes it a second-order element, built on Momentary loudness.
Row: Beat. It pumps once per beat or once per two beats, so its period nests in whole pulses.

listen.label: A kick on every beat, and the pad and the melody duck 9 dB on each kick and swell back over 200 ms. Switch the pump off to hear them steady.

found.summary: We searched the bass stem's level track freely, from 50 ms to 4 s, without telling the detector where the drums are. Then we compared what it found with the pulse measured on a different stem.

chart.title: Pump period in pulses of the drum stem

numbers: Where pumping exists, it nests in whole pulses within 0.5%.
On the track without pumping, the test says no, as it should.

predictions.text: A sidechain pump nests in whole pulses and lives in the Beat row.
predictions.fail: A confirmed pump whose period is not a whole number of pulses.
predictions.evidence: 1 pulse on GRAVITY, 2 pulses on Pure voltage; corrected in issue #5.

Me.sentence: Beats grouped into bars: four in 4/4, three in a waltz, two dotted beats in 6/8.
where: The accented first beat of every bar
The bass note that lands on beat one
The oom-pah-pah of a waltz
place: Column: Periodicity of the accents.

Row: Bar (Z 16 to 18) or Beat. Its Z moves with tempo: a 4/4 bar is in the Bar row below about 120 BPM and in the Beat row above it. That is a fact about the absolute time axis, not an error of the table.
Metric interval: a 4/4 bar is log₂ 4 = 2 above the pulse, a waltz log₂ 3 = 1.585.

listen.label: A pulse with an accent and a low bass note on beat 1 of every 3-beat bar. Switch the meter off to hear the beats all equal.

found.summary: We found the pulse, then measured how strong each beat is and looked for the cycle of strong and weak beats.

chart.title: 4/4 bars measured against tempo, as Z

numbers: The bars at 80.5 and 100 BPM landed at Z 16.58 and 16.26, the values written down before measuring.
A waltz gives 3 beats per bar; a real 6/8 march gives 3 eighths per beat and 2 beats per bar.
In the collider, a rhythm without accents gives no meter.
limits: Meter in a live, tempo-bending performance is not solved: a solo violinist bends the time too much for a fixed-lag method.

predictions.text: The 4/4 bar lands at Z 16.58 at 80.5 BPM and Z 16.26 at 100 BPM.
predictions.fail: Measured bars away from those values.
predictions.evidence: Written in the tempo-series README before those two tracks were measured (commit 069cff0, 2026-11-10 23:15; measured at 23:17 and 23:31). Both came out at those values.

predictions.text: The method finds 3 where 3 is, not only 2 and 4.
predictions.fail: A waltz or a real 6/8 read as binary.
predictions.evidence: Waltz: 3 beats; real 6/8 march: 3 eighths per beat.

Me.pharmakon: Meter checks inside the Track Map tempo.

Hr.sentence: How often the chords change: every bar, every two bars, every four.
where: The chord progression of a pop song
The changes of a blues
A pad or a piano that moves to a new chord on the bar line
place: Column: Change. It asks where something starts or turns: here, the moment a chord turns into the next one.
Row: Bar or Phrase, depending on how many bars a chord holds.
It is measured from the notes only, never from the drums. That makes it an independent test of the metric axis.

listen.label: Not in the collider yet: a chord-change element is planned for the next step.

found.summary: We measured how much the pitch-class content changes at each moment, on the pitched stems only, and looked for the period of those changes.

chart.title: Chord-change period in pulses, by track

numbers: On the four tracks where the chord period is confirmed, it is 4 or 8 pulses: ΔZ = log₂ 4 or log₂ 8 within 0.003.
On three tracks it is not confirmed, so it is not counted.
limits: Confirmed on four of seven tracks. The earlier claim "at every tempo" was too strong and was corrected (issue #7).

predictions.text: Chord changes nest at log₂ of a whole number of pulses.
predictions.fail: A confirmed chord period that is not a whole number of pulses.
predictions.evidence: Held on the 4 of 7 tracks where the period is confirmed; not testable on the other 3.

predictions.text: Generated music changes chords more rigidly than played music.
predictions.fail: A human-played reference shows the same rigidity.
predictions.evidence: A hypothesis; no human reference yet.

Ev.sentence: The outline of a note: how fast its level rises, how it holds and how it dies away.
where: The sharp attack of a plucked string or a piano key
The slow swell of a bowed string or a pad
The decay of a cymbal or a bell
place: Column: Level. It asks how strong the sound is, followed over a few milliseconds.
Row: Tone (Z 6 to 10.7) at its typical 10 ms.
Measured: played faster or slower, its time changes by exactly the same factor and it stays in the Level column, while it moves between rows.

listen.label: Not in the collider yet: an attack and decay element is planned for the next step.

found.summary: We built sounds whose envelope is known exactly, read it back with our own method, and fixed the method and its valid region before one run on held-out sounds.

chart.title: Share of held-out cases read within the criteria

numbers: Inside the region, the time is read with a median error of 0.3%.
A change must last at least 8 periods of the carrier: at the typical 10 ms that means a note above about 800 Hz.
Under tape-speed changes, tones keep their time ratio within 0.55%.
limits: Not checked for noise-like sounds at short times: their own level fluctuates.
A compressed noise carrier failed the time-scaling criterion (up to 7.2%).

predictions.text: Envelope is a Level element near Z 8, for tonal sounds.
predictions.fail: Known envelopes read outside the criteria fixed before the run.
predictions.evidence: Criteria fixed before the runs; 279 of 279 held-out region cells passed.

predictions.text: Envelope time scales exactly with tape speed for every carrier.
predictions.fail: Any carrier off by more than 5%.
predictions.evidence: Held for tones; a compressed noise carrier was off by up to 7.2%.

Ev.pharmakon: Used by the kick onset detector; no general envelope readout yet.

gap:Variation.sentence: How much the bars of a phrase differ from each other: a fill, a small change, a repeat that is played rather than copied.
where: The drum fill at the end of a four-bar phrase
A guitarist who never plays a riff twice the same way
Loop-based music, where it is often almost absent
place: Column: Irregularity. It asks how far from regular something is.
Row: Phrase. A fill that returns every 4 or 8 bars has a period of a whole phrase.

listen.label: A fill closes every 4-bar phrase. Switch Variation off to hear every bar the same.

found.summary: Not yet found in real music. In the collider, the detector compares every bar with the median bar and asks whether the bars that stand out sit on a grid.
numbers: Fills every 4 bars: the detector finds exactly 4 bars.
The same fills in random bars: variation without a period, and no false period.
Across 360 collider settings, pulse, meter and variation are all right in 359.
limits: Only built and detected in our own synthetic sound.

predictions.text: Variation is a measurable element of the Phrase row in real music.
predictions.fail: No real recording shows a confirmed variation period, though its fills are audible.
predictions.evidence: Only in the collider so far.

predictions.text: Loop-based AI music has less variation than played music.
predictions.fail: Generated and played music show the same variation.

gap:Spatial motion.sentence: A sound that travels across the stereo field in a pattern: left, right, and back again.
where: Auto-pan synced to the tempo
The rotating speaker of an organ
Psychedelic and electronic mixes
place: Column: Space. It asks where a sound is, and how signals relate.
Row: Bar. A pan that returns once per bar or two has the period of a bar.

listen.label: The melody travels left to right and back every 2 bars. Switch it off to hear it stay in the middle.

found.summary: Not yet found in real music. In the collider, the detector follows the left–right balance of the melody and looks for its period.
numbers: A cycle of 2 bars is found at 2.00 bars.
With spatial motion switched off, nothing is found.
limits: Only built and detected in our own synthetic sound.

predictions.text: Spatial motion is a measurable element of the Bar row in real mixes.
predictions.fail: Real mixes with audible auto-pan show no confirmed period.
predictions.evidence: Only in the collider so far.

gap:Width arc.sentence: The stereo image opening or closing over a phrase, from mono to wide.
where: A build-up that widens into a drop
A filtered intro that starts in mono
A chorus that is wider than the verse
place: Column: Space.
Row: Phrase. An arc that opens over 8 bars has the period of a phrase.

listen.label: The pad opens from mono to wide over 8 bars, then starts again. Switch it off to hear it stay narrow.

found.summary: Not yet found in real music. In the collider, the detector follows the pad's side-to-mid energy and looks for its period.
numbers: An arc over 8 bars is found at 8.00 bars.
With the arc switched off, nothing is found.
limits: Only built and detected in our own synthetic sound.

predictions.text: Width arc is a measurable element of the Phrase row in real music.
predictions.fail: Real build-ups that audibly widen show no confirmed arc.
predictions.evidence: Only in the collider so far.
